intro: Hi! I'm Iris, the guide of Neo Academia: a city where every neighbourhood teaches something.
Byte is waiting in the Data District, Kernel in Sec and Nova in the AI District. Each of them has a mission for you.
Your car is parked right there on the avenue. Follow the arrow and the minimap. And if you see golden cubes floating around, grab them: they hold facts.
iris.greet: How is it going? You have done {n} of 3 missions. When you finish them all, come back: I have something for you.
graduation: Byte, Kernel and Nova told me everything: you learned to move data, hunt bugs and train with clean data.
That is exactly what we look for: not using technology blindly, but understanding it. Shall we start the ceremony?

topics.a: It's IsAcademy's city: a place to learn by playing. Each district stands for an area: data, networks, security and artificial intelligence.

topics.q: What can I learn at IsAcademy?
topics.a: We give private online classes in Python, SQL, AI, Big Data and Data Engineering for all ages. We start with a free initial assessment to see where you are.
With something small you care about: automating a task, analysing your own data or making a simple game. Python is a great first language: it reads almost like English.

iris.name: Iris

byte.activeReminder: Packets don't deliver themselves! Follow the golden gates before time runs out.
byte.after: Thanks to you, the Neo Academia network is flying. Want to know more about data?

topics.q: What is a piece of data?
topics.a: A recorded fact: a temperature, a click, a sale. Alone it says little; together with others and well organised, it tells stories.
SQL is the language for asking databases questions: "give me sales by country, from highest to lowest". Analysts and AI engineers alike use it.

byte.name: Byte

kernel.activeReminder: There are still bugs on the loose. Look for the red flashes on the map.
kernel.after: Not a bug in sight. Nice work. Shall I tell you something about security?

topics.a: A mistake in a program: the code does what you told it, not what you meant. Debugging is finding that difference with patience and method.

topics.q: How do I protect my accounts?
topics.a: Long, different passwords for every site, a password manager and two-step verification (2FA) whenever you can.

kernel.name: Kernel

nova.activeReminder: Collect clean data (cyan) and dodge the noisy ones (red). The model depends on you.
nova.after: Thanks to you, the model tells signal from noise. Shall we talk about AI?

topics.a: By seeing many examples and adjusting millions of numbers to be wrong less and less often. It doesn't "understand" like you do: it finds patterns.
No. It can be wrong with total confidence. That's why you need to know how to check its answers: AI gives you answers, thinking is up to you.

topics.a: It's the address of a device on a network. Just like a letter needs an address, every data packet needs to know which IP it is going to.
Other companies' computers that you reach over the Internet to store data or run programs. The cloud is made of very real servers.

route.title: Data route
offer: Hi! I'm Byte. Today an important message has to cross the city.
On the Internet, messages travel split into packets, hopping from router to router. You will be that packet: go through the 5 golden gates in order in under two and a half minutes.
route.started: Packet on its way! Go through the golden gates.
steps: Router 1: the message is split into numbered packets.
Router 2: every packet carries the destination IP address.
Router 3: routers choose the next hop, not the whole route.
Router 4: if a path is jammed, packets can take another one.
Destination: packets are put back in order and the message is whole again.
route.lesson: That's how the Internet works: data travels in packets that find their own way and are reassembled on arrival.
route.failed: The packet expired on the way. Real networks would just resend it… and so can you!

debug.title: Debug the city
offer: Kernel here. Three bugs have crept into Neo Academia's systems: find them by their red flashes.
At each one you'll see a piece of Python code with a mistake. Pick the right fix. No rush: debugging is thinking.
debug.started: Hunt the 3 bugs: follow the red flashes.
debug.objective: Bugs fixed: {n}/{total}. Head to the next red flash.
debug.fixed: Bug fixed ({n}/3). On to the next one!
debug.lesson: Debugging means comparing what the code does with what you expected, line by line. Reading error messages calmly is half the solution.
debug.failed: The bugs are still there. Come back any time.

quiz.question: The sum should be 16, but it prints 8.
quiz.code:
numbers = [3, 5, 8]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    total = n
print(total)  # expected: 16
quiz.explain: Exactly! "total = n" replaced the value on every pass; "total += n" adds it up.
quiz.hint: Look at what happens to "total" on each pass of the loop.

quiz.question: The average of 2, 4 and 6 should be 4, but it gives 3.
quiz.explain: Well spotted! The "- 1" was extra. The average is the sum divided by the number of items.
quiz.hint: Work it out by hand: the sum is 12, there are 3 items… what is being subtracted?

quiz.question: The program crashes with "TypeError" when comparing the age.
quiz.explain: That's it! input() always returns text; int() turns it into a number so it can be compared.
quiz.hint: What type of data does input() return? Comparing text with numbers doesn't work.

train.title: Train the model
offer: I'm Nova. I'm training an AI model and I need quality data.
Collect 8 clean data points (cyan) around the streets of the AI District in 2 minutes. Watch out for noisy ones (red): if you grab them, the model will learn worse.
train.started: Collect 8 clean data points (cyan) and avoid the red ones.
train.noisy: Noisy data! The model gets a little confused.
train.resultClean: Model accuracy: {accuracy} %. Not a single noisy point: a textbook training run.
train.resultNoisy: Model accuracy: {accuracy} %. {noisy} noisy data points slipped in and the model notices.
train.lesson: An AI is only as good as its data: garbage in, garbage out. That's why cleaning and choosing data well is half the job.
train.failed: Time's up and the model doesn't have enough data. Another round?
train.resultNoisyOne: Model accuracy: {accuracy} %. 1 noisy data point slipped in and the model notices.

facts.title: The first program (1843)
facts.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine with an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers. It is considered one of the first programs in history.

facts.title: The imitation game
facts.text: In 1950 Alan Turing published "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" and proposed the "imitation game", known today as the Turing test.

facts.title: A name is born
facts.text: The term "artificial intelligence" appears in the 1955 proposal by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.

facts.title: The first "bug" found
facts.text: In 1947 the Harvard Mark II team, where Grace Hopper worked, taped a moth found in a relay into their logbook: "first actual case of bug being found".

facts.title: Python isn't named after the snake
facts.text: Guido van Rossum named his language after the comedy group Monty Python. The first public version came out in 1991.

facts.title: The ENIAC programmers
facts.text: ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers (1945), was programmed by six women, including Jean Bartik and Betty Holberton.

facts.title: "LO": the first message
facts.text: On 29 October 1969 ARPANET sent its first message between UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute (SRI). They meant to type "LOGIN", but the system crashed after "LO".

facts.title: The web was born at CERN
facts.text: In March 1989, at CERN, Tim Berners-Lee proposed the system that would become the World Wide Web.

facts.title: "Just a hobby"
facts.text: In August 1991 Linus Torvalds announced on a forum that he was making an operating system "just a hobby". It was the Linux kernel.

facts.title: Git, in weeks
facts.text: Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005 to manage Linux development. Today it is the most widely used version control system in the world.

facts.title: Moore's law
facts.text: In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of components per chip doubled every year; in 1975 he revised his forecast to every two years.

facts.title: Thinking in true or false
facts.text: In 1854 George Boole published "The Laws of Thought", the basis of the Boolean algebra that digital circuits run on.

facts.title: The perceptron (1958)
facts.text: In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt presented the perceptron, one of the first models of an artificial neuron able to learn from examples.

facts.title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
facts.text: In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue computer defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game chess match.

facts.title: "Attention Is All You Need"
facts.text: This 2017 paper introduced the Transformer architecture, the foundation of today's large language models.

facts.title: The year of AlexNet
facts.text: In 2012 the AlexNet neural network won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin using GPUs, sparking the deep learning boom.

facts.title: Tables and SQL
facts.text: Edgar F. Codd proposed the relational model in 1970 at IBM. That work gave rise to SEQUEL, the forerunner of SQL.

facts.title: The Morris worm
facts.text: In November 1988 the Morris worm spread across the Internet and knocked out thousands of machines. It led to the creation of CERT/CC, one of the first incident response teams.

facts.title: "Hello, world!"
facts.text: The famous first program was popularised by the book "The C Programming Language" (1978) by Kernighan and Ritchie, although it already appeared in a 1972 tutorial by Kernighan.

facts.title: Bits and characters
facts.text: A byte has 8 bits. ASCII, from 1963, used 7 bits: 128 combinations for letters, digits and symbols.

facts.title: The first transistor (1947)
facts.text: In December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, of William Shockley's team at Bell Labs, built the first transistor, the basic building block of every chip.

facts.title: The first microprocessor
facts.text: In 1971 Intel launched the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor: a whole CPU on a single chip.

facts.title: Unicode for every language
facts.text: Unicode 1.0 was published in 1991 so computers could represent the world's writing systems, emojis included today.

facts.title: The first website
facts.text: The first website, info.cern.ch, went online in 1991 and explained what the World Wide Web was.

facts.title: The QR code (1994)
facts.text: Masahiro Hara of the Japanese company Denso Wave invented the QR code in 1994 to track car parts in factories.

facts.title: Wikipedia was born in 2001
facts.text: Wikipedia launched on 15 January 2001 and is now one of the most visited websites in the world, written by volunteers.

facts.title: JavaScript in ten days
facts.text: Brendan Eich created the first prototype of JavaScript in about ten days in May 1995, while working at Netscape.

facts.title: ELIZA, the grandmother of chatbots
facts.text: Between 1964 and 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum created ELIZA at MIT, a program that simulated a conversation with very simple rules.

facts.title: AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol
facts.text: In March 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat go champion Lee Sedol 4–1.

facts.title: Konrad Zuse's Z3
facts.text: In 1941 Konrad Zuse completed the Z3 in Germany, considered the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer.

facts.title: Margaret Hamilton and Apollo
facts.text: Margaret Hamilton led the MIT team that wrote the navigation software for the Apollo missions and popularised the term "software engineering".

facts.title: Hedy Lamarr, actress and inventor
facts.text: In 1942 actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented a frequency-hopping system, a precursor idea of wireless technologies.

facts.title: Python 3
facts.text: Python 3.0 was released in December 2008 and broke compatibility with Python 2 to fix design problems in the language.

facts.title: SQL becomes a standard
facts.text: SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987; that's why almost every database speaks it.

facts.title: Ethernet (1973)
facts.text: Robert Metcalfe and his team invented Ethernet in 1973 at Xerox PARC to connect computers in the same office.

facts.title: The @ in email
facts.text: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between networked computers and chose @ to separate the user from the machine.

facts.title: What is a CAPTCHA?
facts.text: The term CAPTCHA was coined in 2003: it is a test to tell people apart from automated programs.

facts.title: Where "bit" comes from
facts.text: Claude Shannon used the word "bit" (binary digit) in his 1948 paper on information theory and credited the term to John Tukey.

facts.title: Public-key cryptography
facts.text: In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the idea of public keys; RSA followed in 1977 and still protects many connections.

facts.title: Tim Berners-Lee and the first browser
facts.text: Tim Berners-Lee also wrote the first web browser, called WorldWideWeb, on a NeXT computer in 1990–1991.
